title: A head cut and car keys

banner.text: Mike, about 40, blood down his face, keeps asking what happened; he says he's fine and wants to drive home.
He has slid down against the car, eyes closing, snoring.

objective: Apply implied consent for a patient who cannot consent, and recognize when a patient lacks the capacity to refuse
secondaryObjectives: Open the airway with head tilt-chin lift or jaw thrust and insert an oral airway in an unresponsive patient with no gag reflex
Control life-threatening external bleeding with direct pressure, a tourniquet or wound packing
Hand over care to the transporting crew with a concise report

sources.note: Read 2026-11-17: the record page (title, report number, date; the change notices add intramuscular injection, vaccination in a public health emergency and nasal swab collection at EMT and above) and the PDF's skill tables through a summarizing fetch whose table columns were partly unclear, so placement was checked against the course's own reading (backend/supabase/seed/labs/ems-sources.ts, 2026-11-09) and REQ-241's reading (2026-11-11). EMR: oxygen, BVM, naloxone (intranasal or auto-injector), unit-dose hazmat antidote auto-injectors, tourniquet, wound packing, emergency moves, manual stabilization; no pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring or transport. EMT adds pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring, oral glucose, aspirin, the patient's own nitroglycerin, an inhaled bronchodilator, CPAP, the epinephrine auto-injector. AEMT adds IV and IO access, non-medicated IV fluids, supraglottic airways, waveform capnography, sublingual nitroglycerin and a limited list of IV and IM drugs (dextrose, naloxone). Paramedic adds 12-lead interpretation, manual defibrillation, synchronized cardioversion, transcutaneous pacing, needle chest decompression, intubation and medicated infusions. No newer model was found on 2026-11-17.
The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles.

That he decides to drive off about four minutes after you arrive unless you engage him, and that his level of consciousness falls about eight minutes in (as after a head injury with a bleed), are authored for the case. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

brief.situation: 01:30. You are an emergency medical responder on a fire department first-response unit, sent to a bar parking lot: a man fell and hit his head. Mike, about 40, is standing by his car with a bleeding forehead and his keys in his hand. He smells of beer. His friend says he went down hard on the curb about 15 minutes ago.
handover: An ambulance is on the way, about 12 minutes out. Law enforcement can be requested by radio.
Within EMR scope: assessment by hand, bleeding control, airway positioning and adjuncts, and handover. You may not physically restrain him.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated seconds per real second. Pause any time.
Every assessment and treatment takes the time it would on a real call. Scene time and the drive run on the clock.
Partway through you are asked to explain your decisions in writing. The case ends when care is handed over, then a debrief scores what you did.

safetyNote: Teaching case for exam practice; fictional patient. Not medical advice; follow your local protocols and medical direction.

source.note: Unless someone keeps him talking and away from the car, he drives off about 4 minutes after you arrive. Authored for the case; real times vary.
His level of consciousness falls about 8 minutes after you arrive (authored). Authored for the case; real times vary.
Snoring respirations become a blocked airway about 90 seconds later if nobody positions him. Authored for the case; real times vary.
Ambulance 12 minutes out. Authored for the case; real times vary.
A deputy about 5 minutes after the request. Authored for the case; real times vary.
A set of vital signs by hand: about 1 minute. Authored for the case; real times vary.

why.question: He told you he was fine and wanted to go. Why did you not let him, and what are you allowed to do about it?

parts.label: Capacity
parts.criteria: A head injury with confusion, repeated questions and vomiting, plus alcohol, impairs judgment: he is not alert and oriented and cannot understand the risk, so he lacks capacity to refuse and his refusal is not accepted.
parts.modelAnswer: He doesn't know the date, keeps repeating himself and vomited after a head strike, and he has been drinking. He can't understand the risk, so he can't refuse.

parts.label: What I can do
parts.criteria: Treat under implied consent for the emergency; keep him engaged and away from the car without restraining him alone; request law enforcement; the friend holds the keys; contact medical direction if in doubt; never let him drive.
parts.modelAnswer: Care under implied consent, keep him talking on the curb, his friend holds the keys, and a deputy for safety. I don't wrestle him.

reasoningCriteria.label: Written reasoning: capacity and implied consent

expertPath.text: Sit him on the curb with his friend, talking; the friend holds the keys; radio for a deputy.
Capacity: not oriented, repeating himself, vomited, alcohol: he cannot refuse. Pressure on the cut, vital signs.
His consciousness falls and he snores: on his side, jaw thrust if needed, watch his breathing.
Hand over, including the time his consciousness fell and why his refusal was not accepted.

kept.headline: Kept safe, under implied consent
kept.body: A head injury with confusion and alcohol takes away the capacity to refuse. You kept him calm and away from the car without a fight, and caught the airway when he faded.

handed.headline: Handed over, with gaps
handed.body: Check the capacity check, the backup, the bleeding and how fast you positioned his airway.

drove.headline: He couldn't refuse
drove.body: A refusal from a man who doesn't know the date after a head strike is not informed. Keep him talking, keys with his friend, and call law enforcement.

brawl.headline: Don't wrestle him alone
brawl.body: Physical restraint by a single responder hurts both of you. Engage, involve his friend and the deputy.

airway.headline: Snoring is a blocked airway
airway.body: When his consciousness fell, the next step was his side or a jaw thrust within a minute.

scoring.modelReasoning: After a head strike he is confused, repeating himself and has vomited, and he has been drinking: he is not alert and oriented and cannot understand the risk, so he lacks capacity and cannot refuse (NASEMSO: such a patient should not be released at the scene). Treat under implied consent: keep him engaged on the curb, his friend holds the keys, request law enforcement rather than restraining him alone, control the bleeding and take vital signs. When his consciousness falls, position the airway at once (side, jaw thrust) and hand over with the times and why the refusal was not accepted.

cap.ask: While you wait: which finding most clearly means he cannot refuse care?

choices.label: He doesn't know the date and keeps repeating the same question after hitting his head

cap.explain: NASEMSO: capacity means alert, oriented and able to understand the circumstances; judgment significantly impaired by injury or intoxication removes it. Disorientation and repeated questions after a head strike show that impairment; anger alone does not.
